$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse $A^+.$
current_example.worked_solution:
If $A=U_r \Sigma_r V_r ^T$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V_r \, \Sigma_r^+ \, U_r^T,
$$

where $\Sigma_r^+$ is the pseudoinverse of $\Sigma_r.$

First, notice that

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/81cd814ba9845b4cd31cb4f76f190d1af906d21e3693de1d57dea2da61756fd3.svg)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}12 & 16 & 0 \\ 9 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
